headline: Rose mallow blooms on Great Island — stripers hold deep water while the marsh runs the show
subhead: Dog days on the lower Connecticut mean the fish go where the current is, and this week that's the river mouth and not much else.
body_markdown:
The swamp rose mallow is up along Great Island, that big pink hibiscus that only shows itself for about three weeks a year in the high marsh off Old Lyme, and every August I use it the way some men use a calendar. When that bloom opens, I know the river's done giving. The shad are long gone — they ran up past Hartford back in April and May, spawned, and the survivors slipped back out to sea weeks ago. What's left down here at the mouth in August is a different kind of fishing, quieter, hotter, and it asks you to go find cool water instead of waiting for fish to come to you.

I've watched fifty Augusts do this to the lower river, and it never changes much. The flats warm up fast under a high sun, the marsh creeks go nearly bath-water by afternoon, and anything with fins that isn't a mummichog or a killifish pushes down toward where the river dumps into the Sound and the water actually moves. Right now that means Saybrook Point, the mouth itself off Fenwick, the deep cut by the railroad bridge, and the current seams off the DEP Marina. That's where I'm finding stripers, and that's about it — I want to be straight with you, this isn't a week where you can fish anywhere on this river and do well. You have to go to the moving, cooler water or you're wasting bait.

The bass are there, though, and they're not small fish for the most part — schoolies mixed with a decent number of mid-20-inch fish holding on the bottom edge of the deep water off the breakwater, 15 to 22 feet, right where the outgoing tide funnels past the rocks. I've had the best luck starting an hour before the top of the tide and fishing through the first two hours of the ebb, drifting live eels or chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig, letting it sit right on bottom in that current seam where the river water meets the incoming salt. If you'd rather cast, a white or chartreuse 5-inch soft plastic swimming mullet on a 3/4-ounce jighead, worked slow along that same bottom contour, has been drawing strikes from the fish that are actively feeding rather than just holding. Nighttime has been better than daylight this week — the water's cooler, the bass move up shallower to feed, and there's less boat traffic pushing them off the structure.

Great Island and the flats around Lord Cove are holding the summer's other story — snapper blues, thick in the coves where the peanut bunker and silversides have been schooling up in the calmer water off the marsh edges. Small profile lures are the whole game here: half-ounce Deadly Dicks, small Kastmasters, or a bare gold hook with a sliver of bunker under a bobber if you've got kids along, which is really who this bite is for. It's not a trophy fishery, but it's steady, it's fun, and it's happening on the last two hours of the incoming when the bait gets pushed up into those shallow flats.

White perch have gone quiet on me the last couple weeks, which is normal — they've retreated to the deeper holes in the tidal creeks like Selden and Chester Creek and they're feeding mostly at dusk on small nightcrawler pieces or a tiny chartreuse jig worked slow along bottom. If you want white perch in August you fish the last hour of light and the first hour of dark, not midday.

What's really carrying this river right now, if I'm honest, is the blue crabbing. It's about as good as I've seen it in years, especially back in the marsh creeks off Old Lyme and around Lord Cove — chicken necks on a handline, or traps set in three to five feet of water on a falling tide, and you're pulling doubles and triples of legal crabs without much effort. If the fishing's slow some afternoon, that's where I'd send you instead.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the holding pattern at the river mouth would continue and that building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's setting up now. The moon's going new on the 12th, and the tidal range through Saybrook Point and the mouth is already noticeably stronger than it was ten days ago. More water moving through that cut means more bait getting pushed and pulled past the bass holding there, and historically that's when this bite gets from good to very good for about four or five days around the new moon. If I had one window to fish this week, I'd take the outgoing tide the evening of the 11th or the morning of the 12th, right at the breakwater, with eels or bunker chunks on bottom and a bucktail rigged as backup for when the current really starts ripping. Bring bug spray for the greenheads — they're as thick in that marsh grass as I've seen them, and they don't care what the moon's doing.
